title: Negative Marking Strategy
tagline: Year 4 — When a guess pays: expected value with penalties of 1/4, 1/3 and 1/2, and the effect of eliminating options

introduction.overview: Negative marking changes guessing from free to costly. With four options and a penalty of one quarter mark, a blind guess has an expected value of zero; with a penalty of one third it is worse, and with a penalty of one half it is clearly bad. Eliminating options changes this: after removing two options a guess has a 50% chance and a positive expected value. The strategy follows directly: guess only if you can eliminate options or your chance of being right is above the break-even chance.
introduction.placementRelevance: Many tests deduct marks for wrong answers; correct handling of this rule affects the score significantly.
introduction.realWorldContext: Weighing a risky bet against its penalty is the same logic.

learningObjectives: Compute the expected value of a guess
Find the break-even chance for any penalty
Use elimination to raise the chance

coreDefinitions: Penalty: marks deducted for a wrong answer.
Blind guess: a guess without elimination.
Break-even chance: where expected marks are zero.
Expected value: average marks from a choice.
Elimination: removing options you know are wrong.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Guess only when the odds are better than the penalty demands.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Count remaining options k. Chance = 1/k. Compare with the break-even chance n/(m + n).

mainNarrative: Four options, 1 mark, penalty 0.25: blind guess E = 0.25 × 1 − 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.0625, almost zero. With penalty 1/3 the blind guess has E = 0.25 − 0.25 = 0.
With penalty 0.5 a blind guess has E = 0.25 − 0.375 = −0.125.
Remove two options: chance 0.5; with penalty 0.25, E = 0.5 − 0.125 = 0.375, clearly positive.
Break-even chance with penalty 0.25 is 0.25 ÷ 1.25 = 20%; with penalty 1/3 it is 25%; with penalty 0.5 it is 33.3%.
If a section has no negative marking, always answer every question.

deepDiveAspects.title: Fair penalty
deepDiveAspects.content: With k options, a penalty of 1/(k − 1) makes blind guessing exactly fair.

deepDiveAspects.title: Information beats luck
deepDiveAspects.content: A single eliminated option raises the chance from 25% to 33%.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Count options left, compare 1/k with n/(m + n), and guess only if the odds are better.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing blindly with a high penalty

placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Read the penalty rule in the instructions.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Penalty rules differ between tests; always check.
